The first thing my father repaired after he retired was a chair nobody liked.

It had come with the house, abandoned in the cellar by people who had also left six jars of blackened preserves and a calendar from a year in which everyone looked optimistic. The chair was too upright for comfort and too plain to be valuable. One leg ended an inch above the others.

“Firewood,” I said.

“Mostly,” my father agreed.

He carried it upstairs.

Before retirement, he had inspected bridges. He wore white shirts to work and came home with dirt on the cuffs. At dinner, he sometimes described a crack he had seen that day, drawing it on his paper napkin while my mother moved the gravy out of reach of his elbow.

We crossed bridges differently when he drove. He turned the radio down. Once, on holiday, he took a forty-mile detour and refused to tell us why until we were eating lunch.

After retirement, there were no bridges he was authorized to worry about. He began checking the cellar for water. He bought a thermometer for the refrigerator. He asked whether I had ever had the wiring inspected in my apartment.

Then he found the chair.

He set it in the kitchen and spent a morning looking at it.

My mother went around him with the vacuum cleaner.

“Is this where you work now?”

“For the moment.”

“Then your office is on the cord.”

He moved into the garage.

All winter, whenever I visited, the chair stood upside down on his workbench. He took it apart, cleaned the joints, and fitted a new piece of wood to the short leg. The original was beech. His replacement was ash.

“Won’t match,” I said.

“No.”

“You could stain it.”

“Could.”

He didn’t.

In March, he brought the chair into the kitchen. The pale extension looked like a sock on one foot.

My mother sat in it while she peeled an apple. She shifted once, then again.

“Well?” he asked.

“It’s still an uncomfortable chair.”

He pulled it out for himself and finished the apple.

After that came a lamp, a drawer that would not close, and the handle of a saucepan my mother had planned to replace. She had to buy a new saucepan anyway; he kept the old one in the garage for soaking paintbrushes.

Word spread along the street. Mrs. Alvarez brought over a fan that clicked. A boy appeared with a skateboard under his arm and stayed for two hours. Someone left a bread maker on the doorstep with a note that said SOMETIMES SMOKE.

My father wrote back: WHICH TIMES?

He would not let people simply leave things.

“Show me what happens,” he said.

They plugged things in, turned handles, pushed buttons. They made the noises themselves when the machines declined to cooperate.

Most people stayed while he worked. Mrs. Alvarez sat in the repaired chair, which had returned to the garage, and told him about her sister’s hip operation. The boy with the skateboard came back the next Saturday, although his wheels were fine.

Then my father’s hands began to shake.

At first he blamed the cold. He installed a heater. Then he blamed a batch of small screws.

“Cheap heads,” he said, holding one out to me. “Look at that.”

I could see nothing wrong with it, but I looked for a long time.

He started turning work away. He told Mrs. Alvarez her fan needed a specialist. He told the boy, now taller than either of us, that he was getting out of the business.

“You never were a business,” my mother said.

“Well, then. Easy to get out.”

One Saturday, I found him trying to thread a nut onto a bolt. The nut slipped from his fingers and landed somewhere beneath the bench.

Neither of us moved to retrieve it.

Finally he said, “You do it.”

I picked up another nut from the tray.

“Not that one. Different thread.”

I put it down.

He watched as I found the right one and fitted it.

“Don’t force it.”

“I’m not.”

“You are a little.”

We worked for an hour. It was a garden gate latch, bent out of shape by frost or impatience. He held it steady while I tightened the bolts. Then we exchanged places because he didn’t like my angle.

The following week, the boy came back. His name was Daniel. I had never thought to ask.

My father showed him how to replace the cord on a lamp. Daniel did the cutting and stripping. My father checked each connection, leaning close beneath the work light.

By summer, three people were coming regularly. My mother put a kettle in the garage and banned soldering during tea.

The chair finally broke in November.

Mrs. Alvarez leaned back to laugh at something, and one of the old rear legs split. She caught the edge of the bench. Daniel caught her elbow. Her tea went everywhere.

My father knelt beside the pieces.

“Not your leg,” I said, pointing to the pale repair.

He gave me an irritated look.

“Get a towel before she slips.”

We cleared up the tea. Mrs. Alvarez insisted she was fine, then insisted on showing us the bruise already forming on her arm.

When she had gone, my father laid the broken leg on the bench.

Daniel reached for the glue.

“Wait,” my father said. He pulled another chair close and sat down. “Let’s have a look first.”
